content: Lassa fever is an acute viral hemorrhagic illness caused by the Lassa virus, a zoonotic, single-stranded RNA virus. The virus is primarily transmitted to humans through contact with the Mastomys natalensis rodent, which serves as its natural reservoir. This rodent sheds the virus in its urine and feces, which can contaminate food, water, or surfaces. Lassa fever is endemic to West Africa, with an estimated annual incidence of 300,000 to 500,000 cases and a case fatality rate ranging from 5% to 15%. Risk factors for acquiring Lassa fever include travel to endemic regions, exposure to infected individuals or rodents, and occupational exposure in healthcare settings. Pregnant women, immunosuppressed individuals, and young patients are at higher risk of developing complications associated with Lassa fever. After exposure to the virus, the incubation period ranges from 3 to 21 days. Most infected individuals remain asymptomatic or experience mild symptoms. However, symptomatic patients typically present with persistent high-grade fever and other nonspecific symptoms such as headache, myalgia, and vomiting. If untreated, most cases resolve spontaneously, but in some instances, the disease progresses to severe manifestations, including hemorrhage, deafness, edema, seizures, coma, and death. Lassa fever is diagnosed through the detection of Lassa-specific antibodies in the patient’s serum using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Additional diagnostic methods include reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) and immunohistochemistry on tissue samples. Early diagnosis is critical for effective management. The cornerstone of treatment is antiviral therapy with intravenous ribavirin, which is most effective when administered early in the disease course, ideally within the first six days of symptom onset. Ribavirin is given over a 10-day regimen, starting with a loading dose followed by maintenance doses. Supportive care, including maintaining respiratory function, fluid and electrolyte balance, and managing complications, is also essential. There is currently no vaccine available for Lassa fever. Primary prevention involves avoiding contact with Mastomys rodents, particularly in endemic areas, and implementing strict infection control measures to prevent person-to-person transmission in healthcare settings. Proper handling of infected waste and patient secretions is crucial to reduce nosocomial spread. The first documented case of Lassa fever was reported in 1969 following the deaths of two nurses in Lassa, Nigeria. The virus infects endothelial cells and replicates intracellularly using an L-polymerase enzyme and nucleocapsid protein (NP), which helps the virus evade the host immune system. This leads to vascular dysfunction and the clinical manifestations of the disease. The liver is a common target organ, and hepatitis or hepatic necrosis is frequently observed in severe cases. Lassa fever must be differentiated from other diseases that cause hemorrhagic fever or similar symptoms, such as Ebola, typhoid fever, malaria, yellow fever, and shigellosis. The disease is rare in developed countries but remains a significant public health concern in West Africa, where outbreaks can result in case fatality rates as high as 65%. Young age, pregnancy, and immunosuppression are associated with poorer prognosis and increased risk of death. Common symptoms of Lassa fever include persistent high-grade fever, headache, myalgia, arthralgia, cough, conjunctival injection, and vomiting. Severe cases may present with gastrointestinal bleeding, deafness, confusion, seizures, and coma. Physical examination findings often include fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, conjunctival injection, abdominal or chest tenderness, pharyngitis with tonsillar exudates, and hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory findings typically include the presence of IgG antibodies against Lassa virus, detected via ELISA. Monitoring for complications and organ damage is necessary throughout the disease course. Other diagnostic tests, such as RT-PCR and immunohistochemistry, can confirm the diagnosis. Management of Lassa fever includes supportive care and administration of intravenous ribavirin. Ribavirin has been shown to reduce mortality, particularly when given early in the disease course. The treatment regimen involves a loading dose followed by maintenance doses over 10 days. Supportive care focuses on maintaining respiratory status, fluid and electrolyte balance, and addressing complications. Preventive measures include avoiding contact with Mastomys rodents and taking precautions to prevent person-to-person transmission, especially in healthcare settings. This includes proper handling of patient secretions and adherence to infection control protocols.
